name: Barclays

profile.reading:
This facility sits in Middlesex County, New Jersey, near the town of Piscataway, within the same New York City metropolitan corridor of suburban New Jersey that has long hosted back office and data processing operations for major financial institutions. No independently confirmed street address or building name has been documented for this specific location, though the coordinates place it within a stretch of central New Jersey, spanning Middlesex, Somerset, and neighboring counties, that has developed into one of the northeastern United States's denser concentrations of financial sector and telecommunications infrastructure over the past several decades, drawing major banks in search of disaster recovery and data processing capacity outside Manhattan.

Barclays is one of the world's oldest banking institutions, tracing its roots to 1690, when goldsmith bankers John Freame and Thomas Gould began doing business on Lombard Street in London. The bank operated for more than two centuries in various partnership forms before its modern joint stock structure took shape, and it has grown into a global financial services group headquartered in London with substantial investment banking, corporate banking, and technology operations spanning both the United Kingdom and the United States. Barclays significantly expanded its American investment banking footprint in 2008 when it acquired the core North American operations of Lehman Brothers out of that firm's bankruptcy, a deal that brought thousands of employees, trading operations, and associated technology infrastructure needs into the Barclays organization on the US side of the Atlantic.

Firms with that scale of US trading and technology operations typically require dedicated data center capacity outside their primary trading floors, and central New Jersey has been a common choice for banks headquartered in or near New York City for exactly that reason, offering lower costs and ample power availability compared with sites closer to Manhattan, along with fiber connectivity dense enough to support the low latency links trading operations depend on. Beyond that general pattern, no facility specific details, capacity figures, or construction history for this particular Middlesex County site have been confirmed in available public records, and none are asserted here beyond the general, well documented fact of Barclays's large American banking and technology footprint following its post 2008 expansion into the US market.
profile.research_note: Address for this Middlesex County / Piscataway-area point remains unconfirmed. Company history sourced from Barclays' own corporate history page rather than encyclopedia sources. Distinct from a separate Barclays entry elsewhere in this table tagged to Union County, NJ, roughly 13 km away.

profile.address: Cranford, Union County, NJ 07016 (specific street address not publicly confirmed)
profile.reading:
This registry's own coordinates for this site, 40.6437889 north and 74.2854476 west, resolve to Cranford Township in Union County, New Jersey, postal code 07016, according to an independent reverse geocoding lookup performed for this entry. That places the facility in Cranford rather than in Union Township, correcting an earlier address label on this record that simply read Union, Union County, without a specific municipality.

The clearest documented origin for a Barclays owned data center in this part of New Jersey traces to September 2008, when Barclays Capital Inc. acquired the North American investment banking and capital markets business of the bankrupt Lehman Brothers Holdings. Lehman's own 8-K filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, describing the asset purchase agreement, states that the real estate included in that sale comprised Lehman's Seventh Avenue headquarters building in Manhattan together with two data centers located in New Jersey, for a combined real estate price of 1.29 billion dollars, separate from a 250 million dollar payment for other business assets. The filing does not name the two New Jersey data centers individually and does not break out how much of the 1.29 billion dollar figure applied to real estate other than the headquarters tower, so this registry cannot confirm from that document alone that the Cranford site was one of the two, though the timing and Barclays ownership are consistent with this facility having come into Barclays hands through that same 2008 transaction.

No subsequent public filing, town planning record, or NJ Board of Public Utilities filing describing this specific Cranford building, its power capacity, its square footage, or a construction year was located during this research pass. Corporate data centers operated in house by a bank for its own trading and technology operations typically do not publish the kind of spec sheet that colocation providers make available to prospective tenants, and Barclays' own corporate site likewise does not describe individual data center properties.

Barclays as a company traces its history to 1690, when goldsmith bankers John Freame and Thomas Gould began business on Lombard Street in London, according to Barclays' own published company history, with the modern joint stock bank taking shape through an 1896 amalgamation of several country banks. Barclays significantly expanded its United States investment banking and trading presence through the 2008 Lehman acquisition described above, which is the most plausible reason a New Jersey site of this kind would be needed to support American trading and technology operations for a British bank headquartered in London.
profile.acquisition: Acquired by Barclays Capital on 22 September 2008 as part of its purchase of Lehman Brothers North American investment banking and capital markets business. The bankruptcy court set the real estate consideration at 1.29 billion dollars, of which 330 million dollars was for the two New Jersey data centers, Cranford and Piscataway, together; the split between the two sites was not disclosed.
profile.capacity_note: No IT capacity, floor area or power figure for this site has been published by Lehman Brothers, Barclays, or the bankruptcy court record. Private corporate facilities of this kind publish no spec sheet.

reading:
Barclays is a United Kingdom bank, not a data centre company, and it is recorded here as an enterprise private operator for that reason. The facilities carrying its name in this registry are the bank's own infrastructure, built or bought to run its trading, payments and core banking systems, and none of it is leasable space. Its SEC registrants, Barclays PLC under CIK 0000312069 and Barclays Bank PLC under CIK 0000312070, are foreign private issuers rather than US domestic filers, which means their US disclosure is thinner than a domestic registrant's and does not descend to facility level detail.

Why a bank runs its own halls rather than renting them is worth stating, because it explains most of the enterprise private rows in this registry. Trading systems are latency sensitive in ways that make the physical distance between a matching engine and a bank's own servers a business variable. Supervisors impose obligations on operational resilience, data residency and the ability to recover critical functions that are easier to evidence when the bank controls the building. And core banking platforms tend to be long lived systems that are expensive to move, so a data centre acquired decades ago often stays in service long past the point where a cloud native company would have exited it.

The two New Jersey rows in this registry have an unusually specific origin, and it is one of the more revealing numbers in the whole dataset. Barclays acquired Lehman Brothers' North American investment banking and capital markets business out of bankruptcy in September 2008. Two New Jersey data centres came with that purchase, at Piscataway in Middlesex County and Cranford in Union County, which match the two counties recorded here. Reporting at the time of the bankruptcy sale valued those two buildings at about 330 million dollars, against roughly 250 million dollars assigned to the operating business itself. A bank's data centres were worth more than the trading franchise they supported. That is a plain statement of how much of a modern financial institution's value sits in its physical computing infrastructure, and it was made in a bankruptcy court rather than in a marketing brochure.

What is not established is anything about the current state of either building. Barclays publishes no square footage, no utility service figure, no critical IT load, no generator rating and no current operational status for the Piscataway or Cranford sites, and no New Jersey Board of Public Utilities siting case or municipal planning record covering them surfaced in this research. This registry therefore carries both rows without a megawatt figure, and readers should not assume either building still runs at the scale it did in 2008. Separately, Barclays opened a United States technology campus at Whippany in Morris County, New Jersey in July 2018, which its own press release describes as a world class campus and which later local reporting linked to further job growth. Whippany is an office and technology campus rather than a data centre hall, it is in a different county from either registry row, and this entry does not treat it as one of the two facilities recorded here.
